newsitem.title: GERMANY: UK's Cook seeks new era with Bonn and Paris.
newsitem.headline: UK's Cook seeks new era with Bonn and Paris.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook, visiting Bonn and Paris on his maiden trip abroad, said on Wednesday the new government in London wanted to work with the European Union's leading states to shape the community's future.

But Cook, in Germany to meet Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel after a visit to his French counterpart Herve de Charette, was careful to spell out areas where Britain would not join its partners, such as in dropping border controls.

Kinkel praised Labour's landslide victory last week after 18 years of Conservative rule as "a really astonishing victory" and said London and Bonn had common stands on free trade and the need for strong ties with the United States.
But, at a joint news conference, he rejected suggestions that Britain was joining the French-German partnership to form a "tripartite group" leading unity efforts in Europe.
Also on Wednesday, the three countries issued a joint statement supporting a global ban on anti-personnel mines, a step Cook said illustrated the kind of co-operation he sought.

"I want today to be the start of a new era between Britain and the leading members of Europe," Cook told journalists in Bonn. "It is our intention that Britain should now be one of those leading members, not a country on the sidelines seeking to be obstructive."
As part of its "fresh start" in Europe, Britain wanted to work with its EU partners to agree on reforming the Maastricht treaty by the EU summit in Amsterdam next month, he said.
Britain would probably not be in the first wave of states joining the planned economic and monetary union in 1999, he said, but had not ruled out the possibility either.
Asked whether Prime Minister Tony Blair's government was setting a goal to join EMU later, possibly in 2002, Cook would only say: "Not a date."

In Paris, Cook also met French opposition Socialist leader Lionel Jospin. He declined to say whether he would prefer the Socialists or France's ruling centre-right coalition to win the snap parliamentary election on May 25-June 1.
He said the French Socialists were Labour's "sister party" but said: "We will work very closely with whomever the French people choose to govern them."
Cook also met Oskar Lafontaine, chairman of Germany's opposition Social Democrats, after dinner with Kinkel in Bonn.
The two embraced in a comradely bear hug and Lafontaine asked Cook how his Labour party had managed their landslide victory. "It was easy," replied Cook, "You can do the same."

Labour's victory has heartened the French Socialists and German SPD in their electoral battles against conservative governments. France elects a new parliament on May 25 and June 1 while Germany's general election is due in October 1998.
Kinkel, a former head of Germany's liberal Free Democratic Party, thanked Cook warmly for making his first foreign trip to Germany and France.

"It is very important that Paris, London and Bonn are in close contact before the important European decisions we face," he said. "We need a new financial system, a new agricultural system and naturally also need a European currency."
"We are very pleased the new British government is taking a new approach to many issues, especially Europe."
He said Cook had assured him Britain's solidarity in Bonn's dispute with Iran and would not send its ambassador back to Tehran as long as his German counterpart could not return.

Iran said last week neither the German nor the Danish ambassador were welcome to return after the EU agreed to send its envoys back. The EU withdrew its envoys last month after a German court implicated Iranian leaders in the 1992 killing of four Kurdish dissidents in Berlin.
Cook said Britain would consider more majority voting in the EU in certain cases but said other members might now be less interested in scrapping national vetoes.
He said the EU should have "flexibility" -- the code word for majority voting -- in areas such as justice and interior affairs.
As for foreign and security policy, he asked whether it was necessary to introduce majority voting if members had the right to stand aside in what is called constructive abstention.
